title: Latency, percentiles and the tail
goal: By the end you can split a response time into service time and waiting, predict how waiting grows as a server gets busier, report and combine percentiles correctly, catch a load test that hides stalls, and turn a latency target into an SLO with an error budget.

warmup.q: An authorization service needs 10 ms of work per request and is busy half the time; its mean response time is 20 ms. Traffic grows until it is busy 90% of the time. The work per request doesn't change. Roughly what is the mean response time now?
options: About 22 ms, because the work per request is the same
About 36 ms: 1.8 times the traffic, 1.8 times the time
warmup.why: Each request still needs 10 ms of work, but now it usually finds others ahead of it. For one worker with random arrivals, the mean response time is the service time divided by (1 minus utilization): 10 / 0.5 = 20 ms before, 10 / 0.1 = 100 ms after. Waiting grows much faster than traffic, which is why both of the first two answers are too low. A second is where it goes at 99% busy.

sections.h: Response time is service time plus waiting
sections.body:
Your payment service calls a card issuer to authorize a payment, and your dashboard says the call took 120 ms. The issuer's logs say they spent 20 ms on it. Both are right. They measured different things.

The **response time** is what the client sees: from the moment it sends the request until the answer is back. It includes everything. The **service time** is the part when something is actively working on the request: the 20 ms the issuer's code ran. The rest is waiting, either travelling over the network or sitting in a line before anyone picked the request up (queueing delay). In this course, **latency** means that waiting: the time a request is latent, not being worked on. Many people use latency and response time as if they meant the same thing. Keep them apart, because they're fixed in different ways.

Lines form everywhere: in your HTTP client's connection pool, in the kernel's socket buffers (memory where the operating system holds a connection's data), in the server's thread pool, in the database's connection pool, at the disk. Each has the same cause. When requests arrive faster than they can be served, even for a moment, the extra ones wait.

How long they wait depends on how busy the worker is. **Utilization** is the fraction of time a worker is busy, which is the arrival rate times the service time: 50 requests a second at 10 ms each is 0.5, busy half the time. For one worker, with requests that arrive at random and need a random amount of work (the textbook model, called M/M/1), the mean response time is:

```text
mean response time = service time / (1 - utilization)
```

With 10 ms of work per request that's 20 ms at 50% busy, 50 ms at 80%, 100 ms at 90%, 200 ms at 95% and a full second at 99%. Nothing about the requests changed. Each one just found more requests ahead of it. That curve is why a server that looks fine at 70% falls over at 95%, and why capacity plans keep headroom. Making every request take exactly 10 ms helps (the waiting halves) but the curve bends the same way.

One more law ties this together. **Little's law** says that in any stable system the average number of requests inside equals the arrival rate times the average time each one spends inside: L = λ × W. It holds whatever the distributions are. At 2,000 requests a second and 50 ms each, 100 requests are in flight at any moment. That number sizes a thread pool or a connection pool: give the issuer client fewer than 100 connections, and requests queue for a connection before they even leave your machine. That waiting is part of your response time, and the issuer never sees it.

figure.caption: One worker, 10 ms of work per request. The work never changes; the waiting does. At 90% busy the mean response time is 100 ms.

try.title: Push a queue towards 100% busy
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. It simulates one worker in virtual time: a million requests per row, arriving at random, each needing random work with a mean of 10 ms.
Before you run it, predict the mean and the p99 at 95% busy.
Compare the last two columns. They are computed two different ways; why should they agree?

code.title: QueueDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.src:
for (i in 0 until n) {
    t += exp(rnd, meanGap)                           // the next arrival, at random
    val service = exp(rnd, MEAN_SERVICE_MS)          // random work, mean 10 ms
    val start = maxOf(t, freeAt)                     // wait in line if the worker is busy
    freeAt = start + service
    arrive[i] = t
    depart[i] = freeAt
}

try.expect:
```text
one worker, mean service time 10 ms, 1,000,000 requests per row
busy   formula S/(1-p)   measured mean   measured p99   in system   rate x mean
 50%           20 ms           20 ms           92 ms         1.0           1.0
 80%           50 ms           50 ms          231 ms         4.0           4.0
 90%          100 ms           99 ms          442 ms         9.1           8.9
 95%          200 ms          196 ms          924 ms        18.9          18.6
 99%         1000 ms          903 ms         3880 ms        89.3          89.4
90% busy, every request exactly 10 ms: mean 54 ms, p99 215 ms
```

The measured means follow the formula. The 99% row is a little low because at 99% busy the queue swings so widely that a million requests is not enough to average it out. The p99 is about 4.6 times the mean in every row, and it grows just as steeply. The last two columns check Little's law: counting the requests inside the system at 10,000 random moments gives the same number as arrival rate times mean time. The simulation is seeded, so you get exactly these numbers.

sections.h: Averages hide the slow requests, so use percentiles
sections.body:
Here are ten response times from the authorization service, in milliseconds, sorted:

```text
12  13  13  14  15  15  16  18  22  940
```

The mean is 107.8 ms. No request took anywhere near that: nine took 22 ms or less, and one took almost a second. The mean blends the two groups into a number that describes neither.

Read positions off the sorted list instead. The **median**, or p50, is the middle value: half the requests were faster, half slower. Here it's 15 ms, what a typical user waits. The **p99**, the 99th percentile, is the value that 99% of requests were at or below, and p999 is the same for 99.9%. These high percentiles describe the **tail**, the slow end of the distribution. Ten values can't tell you a p99; collect thousands first.

Why care about one request in a hundred? Because the users who hit it are often the ones who matter most. The slowest requests tend to belong to the customers with the most data, such as the merchant with the biggest catalogue. Amazon set its internal targets at p99.9 for that reason (the Dynamo paper, 2007). And a page that makes many backend calls hits the tail on most loads, which section 4 works out.

Percentiles have one trap: you can't average them. Ten pods serve the same API and get equal traffic. Nine have a p99 of 25 ms. The tenth shares a machine with a noisy neighbour, another busy program, and 15% of its requests take 900 ms, so its p99 is 900 ms. The average of the ten p99s is 113 ms. The real p99 of the service is 900 ms, because the bad pod's slow requests are 1.5% of all traffic, more than the 1% a p99 leaves out. Averaging can be wrong in the other direction too; the lab has a case where it says 412 ms and the truth is 25 ms.

The fix is to keep counts, not percentiles. A **histogram** splits the range of possible values into buckets and counts how many requests fell into each. Counts add: merge the ten pods' histograms bucket by bucket and you have the histogram of the whole service, from which you can read any percentile. Good buckets are narrow for small values and wide for large ones. If each bucket is about 2% wider than the one before (logarithmic buckets), every value the histogram reports is within 1% of a value really recorded, and about 1,100 buckets cover 1 µs to an hour. HdrHistogram, by Gil Tene, and DDSketch, from Datadog, are production versions of this idea, and the lab builds one.

Tools get this wrong in two ways. A Prometheus summary computes quantiles inside each process, and the Prometheus docs say averaging them gives statistically nonsensical values. A Prometheus histogram aggregates correctly, but its classic buckets are few and fixed, so a percentile is only as precise as the bucket it falls in: in the docs' own example the true p95 is about 220 ms and the estimate is 295 ms.

try.title: Average ten p99s, then do it properly
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. Ten pods, 10,000 requests each; pod 9 is slow for 15% of its requests.
Before the last three lines print, write down your guess for the service's real p99.
Change `15` to `9` in `PercentileDemo.kt` and run it again. Which of the two p99 lines moves?

code.title: PercentileDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.src:
val averagedP99 = pods.map { quantile(it, 0.99) }.average()
val all = pods.flatMap { it.asList() }.toLongArray().also { it.sort() }   // what merging histograms gives you
println("average of the ten p99s:  %.0f ms".format(averagedP99))
println("p99 of all %,d requests: %d ms".format(all.size, quantile(all, 0.99)))

try.expect:
```text
pod   requests   mean    p50    p99
  0      10000     18     18     25
  1      10000     19     19     25
  ...
  8      10000     18     18     25
  9      10000    157     20    900

average of the ten p99s:  113 ms
p99 of all 100,000 requests: 900 ms
service mean 32 ms, p50 19 ms, p90 24 ms, p99.9 900 ms
```

(output trimmed). Pod 9's p50 is 20 ms, like the others: most of its requests are fine. Its slow 15% are 1.5% of all traffic, which is more than the 1% a p99 leaves out, so the service's p99 is 900 ms while the averaged figure says 113 ms. With 9% instead of 15%, the slow requests would be 0.9% of the traffic, the true p99 would drop to about 25 ms, and the average of p99s would still say 113 ms: wrong in the other direction. Note the mean, 32 ms: it hides the problem completely.

sections.h: The lying load test: coordinated omission
sections.body:
You want to know how the authorization service behaves at 1,000 requests a second, so you run a load test. The usual tool works like this: open 10 connections, and on each one send a request, wait for the answer, record how long it took, then send the next, each connection paced at 100 requests a second. The report says p99 = 6.23 ms.

Now freeze the server for 1.4 seconds in the middle of the run, the way a long garbage-collection pause would, and test again. The report barely changes: p99 = 9.02 ms. Only the max, 1.40 s, gives the pause away. Real users would have seen something very different. They don't wait for each other. At 1,000 a second, 1,400 of them would have arrived during the pause, and each would have waited up to 1.4 seconds.

The load generator stopped sending while the server was stuck. Each of its 10 connections had one request in flight, waited 1.4 s for it, and recorded one slow sample. The 1,400 requests that should have gone out during the pause were sent late, after the server woke, and timed from when they finally went out, so they look fast. In effect the generator agreed with the server not to measure during the bad period. Gil Tene named this **coordinated omission**.

A generator that waits for each answer before sending the next request uses a **closed model**. One that sends at a fixed rate, whatever the server is doing, uses an **open model**, and that is how users behave. The k6 load-testing docs show the difference with an endpoint that takes 6 seconds to answer: over one minute, the closed model with one virtual user completes about 10 iterations, while the open model at one per second starts 60, using up to 11 virtual users at once.

There are two fixes. Use an open model and time every request from when it was scheduled to go out (wrk2 with `-R`, k6's `constant-arrival-rate`). Or keep the closed loop but time each request from its planned send time rather than its actual one, which is what wrk2 calls correction; HdrHistogram's `recordValueWithExpectedInterval` does the same after the fact. In this lesson's simulation both give p99 = 1.28 s. wrk2's README shows the real thing: with a 1.4 s pause, the corrected p99 is 1.27 s and the uncorrected one 6.04 ms, about 200 times smaller.

A JUnit test that loops on 50 threads and times each call falls into the same trap. It measures a closed system's service time, not what your users wait.

try.title: Run the lying load test
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. It runs three load generators against a simulated server, first quiet, then with a 1.4 s freeze at t = 10 s.
Predict the closed model's p99 with the freeze before you look.
Find the one column where the closed run, timed from the actual send, admits that something happened.

code.title: LyingLoadTestDemo.kt (excerpt)

try.expect:
```text
-- quiet server
                               count        p50        p90        p99      p99.9        max
closed, timed from send        30000    0.51 ms    3.16 ms    6.23 ms    8.50 ms   10.82 ms
closed, timed from plan        30000    0.51 ms    3.16 ms    6.23 ms    8.50 ms   10.82 ms
open, fixed arrival rate       30000    0.51 ms    3.16 ms    6.23 ms    8.50 ms   10.82 ms
-- server frozen for 1.4 s at t=10 s
                               count        p50        p90        p99      p99.9        max
closed, timed from send        30000    0.54 ms    4.58 ms    9.02 ms   12.79 ms     1.40 s
closed, timed from plan        30000    0.54 ms     0.18 s     1.28 s     1.39 s     1.40 s
open, fixed arrival rate       30000    0.54 ms     0.18 s     1.28 s     1.39 s     1.40 s
```

On a quiet server all three agree. With the pause, the closed run timed from the actual send hides it everywhere except the max. Timed from the plan, the same closed run matches the open one. The p90 of 0.18 s is the backlog: after the pause the one worker needs a while to catch up with 1,400 queued requests while new ones keep arriving. The run happens in virtual time, so it takes a fraction of a second and always prints these numbers.

sections.h: Fan-out makes the tail the common case
sections.body:
A merchant opens their dashboard. To draw it, the backend asks 100 services, or 100 shards (pieces of one database split across machines), for a piece each, in parallel, and waits for all of them. Each of these leaves is quick: 5 to 15 ms, except one time in a hundred, when it hits a pause and takes a full second. What does the merchant see?

The page is slow if any one leaf is slow. The chance that all 100 are fast is 0.99^100 = 0.366, so 63% of page loads take a second or more. A tail that touched 1% of one leaf's calls now touches most users. Jeff Dean and Luiz André Barroso described this in "The Tail at Scale" (2013), with the same arithmetic: a server that usually answers in 10 ms but takes a second at its p99 makes 63% of requests slow at a fan-out of 100. Even at one slow call in 10,000, a fan-out of 2,000 makes almost one user request in five slower than a second. In a real Google service they measured, one random leaf finished at p99 in 10 ms, but waiting for all the leaves took 140 ms at p99. This is **tail latency amplification**. It means a leaf needs a far stricter target than the user-facing service: to keep only 1% of pages slow at a fan-out of 100, each leaf may be slow only 0.01% of the time.

You can't make every leaf perfect, but you can stop waiting for the unlucky one. A **hedged request** sends a second copy of a slow call to another replica (a server holding a copy of the same data) and takes whichever answer arrives first. Send the hedge only once the call has been out longer than the leaf's p95, and it adds at most about 5% more requests. In the paper's test, reading 1,000 keys spread over 100 servers of BigTable, Google's large table store,, hedging after 10 ms cut the p99.9 from 1,800 ms to 74 ms and sent only 2% more requests. A **tied request** goes further: it queues the request on two servers at once, each told about the other, and whichever starts first cancels its twin.

Hedging works under two conditions. Slowness must strike replicas independently: if the cause is shared, such as the same bad deploy on every replica or one overloaded disk under all of them, the hedge is slow too. And the request must be safe to run twice, which is called **idempotent**. A read is idempotent; a card authorization is only if it carries an idempotency key that the issuer checks. gRPC supports hedging per method in its service config (`hedgingPolicy`, at most 5 attempts), and its guide warns that hedged methods must be idempotent.

try.title: Fan out, then hedge
steps: Run the demo below from the `labs` folder. Each simulated page fans out to N leaves; a leaf takes 5 to 15 ms, or 1 s one time in 100.
Predict the share of slow pages at 100 leaves before it prints.
Predict what hedging after 15 ms does to the p99 and to the p99.9, and how many extra requests it costs. Then look at the last row: why does hedging stop working there?

code.title: FanOutDemo.kt (excerpt)
code.src:
val latency = if (hedgeAfter == null || first <= hedgeAfter) first
              else { hedges++; minOf(first, hedgeAfter + second) }   // first answer wins
slowest = maxOf(slowest, latency)                                     // the page waits for all leaves

try.expect:
```text
leaves   slow requests   formula 1 - 0.99^N
     1            1.1%                 1.0%
    10            9.5%                 9.6%
   100           63.2%                63.4%
  1000          100.0%               100.0%

100 leaves                     p50       p99     p99.9   extra requests
no hedging                  1000 ms    1000 ms    1000 ms        0.0%
hedge after 15 ms             23 ms      30 ms    1000 ms        1.0%
hedge, slowness shared      1000 ms    1000 ms    1000 ms        1.0%
```

With 100 leaves even the median page takes a second. Hedging after 15 ms (later than any fast leaf) sends 1% more requests and brings the p99 down to 30 ms. The p99.9 stays at a second: one leaf call in 10,000 has both copies slow, and with 100 leaves that happens on 1% of pages. When the slowness is shared, the hedge is just as slow and buys nothing for the same 1% of extra load.

sections.h: SLOs and error budgets turn the tail into a target
sections.body:
Knowing your p99 helps only once you've decided what it should be. Google's SRE books give the words most teams now use.

A **service level indicator** (SLI) is a precisely defined measurement: for the authorization API, "the fraction of authorization requests, measured at the load balancer (the machine that spreads requests across your servers), that get a non-error answer within 300 ms". Where you measure is part of the definition. At the load balancer you see the queueing and the network; inside the server you don't.

A **service level objective** (SLO) is a target for an SLI over a time window: "99.9% of authorization requests are good, over 30 days". Latency objectives are often given at several percentiles, to pin down the shape: 99% under 300 ms and 99.9% under 1 s. An **SLA** is an SLO written into a contract with consequences, such as refunds or credits. If nothing happens when you miss it, it is an SLO.

The 0.1% that may go wrong is the **error budget**. Over 30 days, 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes of complete outage, or 0.1% of requests failing all month, or any mix of the two. 99.99% allows 4.32 minutes, and 99.999% about 26 seconds. The budget turns arguments into arithmetic: if little of it is used, ship the risky migration; if it's nearly gone, slow releases down and fix reliability. Don't run far ahead of it either. Google's Chubby, a lock service other systems use to coordinate, was so reliable that other teams built in the assumption that it never failed, so its owners took it down on purpose in any quarter where it had beaten its SLO.

Alert on how fast the budget is going. The **burn rate** compares how fast you are spending the budget with the steady pace that would spend exactly all of it by the end of the window, so a burn rate of 1 uses the whole budget in 30 days. The SRE Workbook recommends paging when the burn rate over the last hour is 14.4 (that hour alone used 2% of the month's budget) or over the last 6 hours is 6 (5%), and opening a ticket when it is 1 over 3 days (10%). Each alert also checks a short window (5 minutes for the one-hour alert) so it stops firing soon after the problem does. A total outage burns at 1,000 and empties a 99.9% budget in about 43 minutes. Paging on every error spike instead can wake someone up to 144 times a day while the service still meets its SLO.

try.title: Spend an error budget by hand
steps: Your authorization API has an SLO of 99.95% good requests over 30 days and serves a steady 1,200 requests a second.
1. How many failed requests does the month's budget allow?
2. A bad deploy makes 3% of requests fail for 20 minutes, then it's rolled back. What burn rate is that, and how much of the budget did it use?
3. Would the one-hour page (burn rate 14.4 over the last hour, and over the last 5 minutes) have fired before the rollback? When?
try.expect:
1. 30 days is 2,592,000 seconds, so the API serves 1,200 × 2,592,000 = 3,110,400,000 requests. 0.05% of that is **1,555,200 failed requests**. As time, a total outage would use it up in 21.6 minutes.
2. 3% failing against a 0.05% allowance is a **burn rate of 60**. In 20 minutes the API served 1,440,000 requests, and 3% of them, 43,200, failed: **2.8% of the month's budget**.
3. Over the one-hour window the burn rate climbs by 1 for every minute of the incident (60 × minutes ÷ 60), so it passes 14.4 after about **14.4 minutes**, and the 5-minute window is far above 14.4 by then. The page fires about 14 minutes in, before the rollback at 20 minutes. The 6-hour rule needs 36 minutes at this rate and never fires.

If you got 60 minutes of budget used for question 2, you multiplied the duration by the burn rate in minutes but forgot to divide by the window: 20 × 60 = 1,200 minutes of budget-pace, out of 43,200 minutes in 30 days, is the same 2.8%.

refs.title: Google SRE book: Service Level Objectives
Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs

analogy: A server is a supermarket with one till. Each customer takes about a minute to check out. When customers arrive at random and the cashier is busy half the time, you wait about a minute on top of your own; at 90% busy the line is usually several people long and the average wait is nine minutes, though nobody's shopping got bigger. The p99 is the customer stuck behind someone paying in coins, and a manager who reads only the average never hears about them. The analogy breaks at fan-out: no shopper has to queue at 100 tills and wait for the slowest one, but a dashboard request that calls 100 services does exactly that.
in_your_world: Take your Quarkus authorization service. If it publishes timers to Prometheus, turn on percentile histograms (Micrometer's `publishPercentileHistogram()`) and build dashboards that merge buckets across pods with `histogram_quantile` over summed bucket rates, instead of averaging each pod's p99. Size the HTTP client's connection pool to the card issuer with Little's law: at 400 authorizations a second and 120 ms each, about 48 calls are in flight, so a pool of 20 makes requests queue for a connection inside the JVM, and that wait shows up as response time the issuer never sees. When you load test with Gatling or k6, use an open model with a fixed arrival rate, or a GC pause will vanish from the report. And where a request fans out (a dashboard that calls six services, a Temporal workflow that waits for several activities), give each dependency a stricter latency target than the user-facing one, and hedge only calls that are safe to repeat.
mistake: The most common mistake is trusting the p99 from a closed-loop load test. It happens because most tools default to closed loops, and so does every hand-written test that starts some threads and has each one send, wait and time. When the server stalls, the generator stalls with it, the stall leaves a handful of slow samples, and the report looks healthy until the first long GC pause in production. Use an open model with a fixed arrival rate (wrk2 `-R`, k6 `constant-arrival-rate`, Gatling's open injection profiles), time each request from its scheduled start, and read the max next to the p99: a max far above the p99.9, with a clean p99, is the signature of coordinated omission.

compare.title: A closed load loop and an open one

a.label: Closed model
a.title: waits for each answer

b.label: Open model
b.title: sends on schedule

compare.note: Both loops aim at the same rate. The closed one can't send its next request until the previous answer is back, so during a 1.4 s pause it sends nothing and records a single slow sample. The open one keeps launching requests on virtual threads at their planned times and times each from its slot, so every request that should have gone out during the pause is counted with the wait it really had. `Client` stands for your HTTP client, and `LogHistogram` is this lesson's lab.

worked.title: Read the p99 of two pods from their histograms

steps.say: Two pods report histograms with six buckets, labelled by their upper bound in ms. Pod A served 10,000 requests and pod B 2,000.

Each pod's own p99 is the bucket where the running total reaches 99% of its count. Pod A needs rank 9,900: 4,000, then 9,800, then 9,950, so its p99 is in the 50 ms bucket. Pod B needs rank 1,980 and only gets there in the last bucket.
The tempting shortcut averages the two: (50 + 1,000) / 2 = 525 ms. It ignores that pod B serves a sixth of the traffic, and the true answer can't be computed from two percentiles anyway.
Merge instead: add the counts bucket by bucket, then read the p99 of the whole. Rank ceil(0.99 x 12,000) = 11,880 falls in the 100 ms bucket.

So the service's p99 is between 50 and 100 ms, not 525. Note the "between": with buckets this wide you only know the range, which is the bucket-width error the Prometheus docs warn about. Logarithmic buckets 2% apart narrow it to within 1%.
steps.code: true p99 in (50 ms, 100 ms]; the averaged figure was 5 to 10 times too high

lab.title: Build a mergeable histogram and catch a lying load test
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 19 fail with `NotImplementedError`.

In `LogHistogram.kt`, read `bucketIndex` and `bucketValue`: they hold the logarithmic bucket arithmetic. Write `record`, then `quantile`, then `merge`. The 7 tests in `LogHistogramTest` should pass, including a jqwik property that checks every quantile against the exact one on 30 random data sets.

In `LoadTest.kt`, read `PausingServer` (a one-worker server in virtual time that can freeze) and `closedLoop`. Then write `openLoop`: request i goes out at `i * 1_000_000 / ratePerSec` µs whatever the server is doing, and its latency is answer time minus send time.
Run `LyingLoadTestTest`. Through the 1.4 s freeze the closed model's p99 stays under 10 ms; yours goes over a second.
In `FanOut.kt`, write `rootLatency`: each leaf's latency with or without a hedge, and the slowest of them. Run all the tests until they pass.
hints: `quantile`: return 0 if `count == 0L`. Otherwise `val rank = maxOf(1L, ceil(q * count).toLong())`, add up `counts[i]` from i = 0, and at the first i where the total reaches `rank` return `minOf(bucketValue(i), max)`.
`openLoop`: loop over a `Long` i and compute `val sendAt = i * 1_000_000L / ratePerSec`; stop when `sendAt >= durationMicros`. With an `Int` i, `i * 1_000_000` overflows after about 2,147 requests.
`rootLatency`: a leaf is hedged only when `hedgeAfter != null && c.first > hedgeAfter`, and its latency is then `minOf(c.first, hedgeAfter + c.second)`.

drill.title: The three formulas, from memory
drill.prompt: Without notes: (1) a leaf is slow 1% of the time; what fraction of requests is slow at a fan-out of 10, 100 and 1,000? (2) How rarely may each leaf be slow if only 1% of requests at a fan-out of 100 may be slow? (3) Write the mean response time of one worker at utilization ρ, and its value at 90% busy for 10 ms of work. (4) Write Little's law and use it for 400 requests a second at 120 ms.

answer.src:
(1) P(slow) = 1 - 0.99^N
    N = 10:     1 - 0.904   = about 10%
    N = 100:    1 - 0.366   = about 63%
    N = 1,000:  1 - 0.00004 = almost 100%
(2) 1 - (1 - p)^100 = 0.01  ->  (1 - p)^100 = 0.99  ->  p = about 0.0001
    each leaf may be slow 0.01% of the time: its p99.99 has to meet the page's p99 target
(3) W = S / (1 - ρ)
    10 ms / (1 - 0.9) = 100 ms
(4) L = λ × W
    400 per second × 0.12 s = 48 requests in flight

recap: Response time is what the client waits: service time plus latency, the time spent travelling and queueing. Measure it at the client.
Waiting grows like 1 / (1 - utilization): 10 ms of work takes 100 ms on average at 90% busy. Little's law (L = λ × W) sizes pools.
Report percentiles, not the mean. Never average percentiles; merge histograms and read the percentile from the merged counts.
A closed-loop load test stops sending when the server stalls and hides the stall (coordinated omission). Use an open model and time requests from their scheduled start.
Fan-out turns a rare tail into the common case (1 - 0.99^100 = 63%). Hedged requests buy it back for a few percent more load, if replicas fail independently and the call is idempotent.
An SLO is a target for an SLI over a window; what it allows to fail is the error budget. Page on fast burn rates, not on every error.

quiz.q: Ten pods get equal traffic and report p99s of 20, 22, 21, 19, 25, 20, 23, 21, 22 and 400 ms. What can you say about the service's p99?
options: It's 59.3 ms, the average of the ten
It's 21.5 ms, the median of the ten
Not enough from these numbers: merge the pods' histograms and read it from the result
quiz.why: Percentiles don't combine. The service's p99 depends on how much of all traffic is slow, which ten p99s don't tell you. If 1% of the slow pod's requests are near 400 ms, that's 0.1% of all traffic and the service's p99 is near 25 ms; if 15% are, it's 400 ms. The average looks like an answer, which is the trap. Only merged counts give the real one.

quiz.q: A load test with 50 threads, each looping send, wait, record, reports p99 = 12 ms. In production the p99 is 900 ms around GC pauses. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Production traffic is heavier than the test's
The test is a closed model: it stopped sending during pauses, so only about 50 samples per pause were slow
The test machine's clock is wrong
A p99 isn't meaningful below 100,000 samples
quiz.why: Each of the 50 threads has one request in flight when the server pauses and records one slow sample, then sends its overdue requests late and times them from the late send. That's coordinated omission. Heavier traffic could also raise the p99, but it wouldn't explain a test that saw the same pauses and reported almost nothing.

quiz.q: A checkout page calls 20 services in parallel and waits for all of them. Each is slower than 500 ms 0.5% of the time, independently. Roughly what fraction of page loads take longer than 500 ms?
quiz.why: The page is slow if any call is: 1 - 0.995^20 = 1 - 0.905, about 9.5%. The first answer is the tempting one because each service is fast 99.5% of the time, but the page needs all 20 to be fast at once.

quiz.q: Your service has a 99.9% SLO over 30 days. A deploy makes every request fail for 10 minutes before it's rolled back. How much of the month's error budget did that use?
quiz.why: The budget is 0.1% of 30 days, 43.2 minutes of total outage. Ten minutes of 100% errors is a burn rate of 1,000 for 10 minutes, which is 10 / 43.2 = 23% of the budget. One bad deploy like that a month leaves room for three more.

quiz.q: Lesson 1 split work into operational and analytical. Where does an SLO of "99% of requests under 300 ms" make sense?
options: The authorization API that checkout calls
quiz.why: A per-request latency percentile fits operational work: many small requests from code that waits for each answer. The other three are analytical or batch work, a few big jobs where the useful objective is about completion or freshness (settlement done by 06:00, the warehouse no more than a day behind), not a per-request p99.

flashcards.front: Response time vs service time vs latency?
flashcards.back: Response time is what the client waits, end to end. Service time is the part spent working on the request. Latency (in this course) is the waiting: network transit plus queueing.

flashcards.front: Mean response time of one worker at utilization ρ?
flashcards.back: S / (1 - ρ) for random arrivals and random work (M/M/1). 10 ms of work: 20 ms at 50% busy, 100 ms at 90%, 1 s at 99%.
Requests in the system = arrival rate × time each spends there (L = λW). 2,000 requests a second × 50 ms = 100 in flight.

flashcards.front: Why can't you average p99s across pods?
flashcards.back: A percentile depends on the whole distribution. Merge the pods' histograms (add the bucket counts) and read the p99 from the merged counts.

A closed-loop load generator stops sending while the server stalls, so the stall shows up in a handful of samples and the p99 looks fine. Fix: an open model at a fixed rate, timed from the planned send.

flashcards.front: Fan-out of 100, each leaf slow 1% of the time: what fraction of requests is slow?
The error budget of a 99.9% SLO over 30 days?
flashcards.back: 0.1% of requests, or 43.2 minutes of total outage. A burn rate of 14.4 for one hour spends 2% of it.

terms.plain: How long the client waits for an answer, from sending the request to receiving the reply.
The part of the response time when something is actively working on the request.
The fraction of time a worker is busy: arrival rate times service time.
The value that the given share of requests were at or below. p50 is the median; p99 describes the slow tail.
A load test that stops sending while the server stalls, and so hides the stall from its results.
A second copy of a slow call, sent to another replica after a delay; the first answer wins.
A target for a measured service level (an SLI) over a time window, such as 99.9% of requests good over 30 days.
What an SLO allows to go wrong: 0.1% of requests for a 99.9% SLO.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate shows you a load-test report with p99 = 8 ms and says the service is ready for the holiday peak. Explain what you would check before believing it.
explain_back.answer: First, how was the load generated? If the tool keeps a fixed set of connections that each wait for an answer before sending the next request, it stops sending whenever the server stalls, so a GC pause shows up as a few slow samples and the p99 stays low. I'd want an open model at a fixed arrival rate, with each request timed from its scheduled start, and I'd look at the max next to the p99: a max of a second with a p99 of 8 ms is the giveaway. Second, at what utilization? The peak will push the servers much harder, and waiting grows like 1 / (1 - utilization), so a p99 measured at 50% busy says little about 90%. Third, where was it measured and how was it combined: at the client, across all pods by merging histograms, not by averaging each pod's p99. And last, what does the page do with it? If one user request fans out to many calls, the user's p99 is far worse than each call's.

deeper.body:
**The p99 is a warning light more than a speedometer.** Marc Brooker points out that high percentiles are dominated by queueing, so they rise with load whatever the code does. That makes them a poor measure of whether a change made the code faster, and a good early sign that a system is near overload. To judge efficiency he suggests the mean (or the service time itself). Use both, for different questions.

**Better sketches.** The lab's histogram is the core of DDSketch (Masson, Rim and Lee, VLDB 2019): logarithmic buckets that guarantee a relative error, so a p99.9 of 1.8 s is reported within 1% of 1.8 s, and sketches merge by adding counts. Rank-error sketches such as t-digest guarantee something different, an error in the rank, which on very skewed latency data can still mean a large error in the reported value. HdrHistogram fixes precision in significant digits instead: three digits from 1 µs to an hour take about 185 KB and record in constant time. Prometheus's newer native histograms also use exponential buckets, and its docs now recommend them over both classic histograms and summaries.

**Tied requests in numbers.** In "The Tail at Scale", BigTable reads with a tied request sent after 1 ms on a mostly idle cluster went from p50 19 ms to 16 ms and from p99.9 98 ms to 61 ms. With a large sort job running on the same machines, the p99 fell from 108 ms to 67 ms, while the extra disk work stayed under 1%. The paper's other techniques include taking slow machines out of rotation while still sending them shadow requests (latency-induced probation) and sending a risky request to one or two leaves first (canary requests). Lesson 3 meets both again.

The framing of response time, service time and percentiles follows Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 2. Coordinated omission is not in that chapter; the wrk2 and k6 docs cover it.
